nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-02.title: Subtract three sectors
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-02.body:
The triangle has area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot2^2=\sqrt3$. Inside the triangle, each unit circle covers a $60^\circ$ sector of area $\frac16\pi$; the circles touch only at the midpoints of the sides, so the sectors do not overlap. The remaining area is $\sqrt3-3\cdot\frac{\pi}{6}=\sqrt3-\frac{\pi}{2}$.

**Answer: $\left(\sqrt3,-\frac12\right)$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-03.title: Binary search
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-03.body:
With $g$ guesses one can guarantee finding the number among at most $2^g-1$ possibilities: the first guess splits the rest into two parts, each searchable with $g-1$ guesses, so $N(g)=2N(g-1)+1$ with $N(1)=1$. Since $2^{10}-1=1023<2000\le2047=2^{11}-1$, $10$ guesses cannot guarantee success but $11$ can (always guess the middle of the remaining range).

**Answer: $11$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-04.title: Count factors of 5
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-04.body:
The number of trailing zeros of $k!$ is $Z(k)=\lfloor k/5\rfloor+\lfloor k/25\rfloor+\lfloor k/125\rfloor+\lfloor k/625\rfloor$.

$Z(1999)=399+79+15+3=496$, while $Z(2000)=400+80+16+3=499$, and $Z$ never decreases. So $k=1999$ is the largest with exactly $496$ zeros (in fact $k=1995,\dots,1999$ all give $496$).

**Answer: $1999$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-06.title: Along the diagonal
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-06.body:
Put $A$ at the origin with sides along the axes. The inscribed circle has center $(2,2)$ and radius $2$. A circle of radius $s$ tangent to both sides at $A$ has center $(s,s)$, and external tangency to the big circle requires
$$(2-s)\sqrt2=2+s\ \Rightarrow\ s=\frac{2\sqrt2-2}{\sqrt2+1}=2(\sqrt2-1)^2=6-4\sqrt2.$$

**Answer: $6-4\sqrt2$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-06.title: Ratio along the diagonal
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-06.body:
From corner $A$ to the inscribed circle's center is $2\sqrt2$, so the gap from $A$ to the inscribed circle is $2\sqrt2-2$. A circle of radius $s$ in the corner reaches $s\sqrt2+s$ from $A$ along the diagonal. Setting $s(\sqrt2+1)=2\sqrt2-2$ gives $s=2(\sqrt2-1)^2=6-4\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $6-4\sqrt2$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-07.title: List the possible numbers
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-07.body:
The possible numbers are $10a+b$ with $6\ge a\ge b\ge1$: there are $21$ of them. Their sum is
$$\sum_{a=1}^{6}\sum_{b=1}^{a}(10a+b)=\sum_{a=1}^6\left(10a^2+\frac{a(a+1)}{2}\right)=910+56=966.$$
The average is $\frac{966}{21}=46$.

**Answer: $46$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-07.title: Average digits
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-07.body:
For tens digit $a$ there are $a$ numbers, so the tens digit averages $\frac{\sum a^2}{21}=\frac{91}{21}=\frac{13}{3}$. The units digit $b$ appears $7-b$ times, so it averages $\frac{\sum b(7-b)}{21}=\frac{56}{21}=\frac83$. Average number: $10\cdot\frac{13}{3}+\frac83=\frac{138}{3}=46$.

**Answer: $46$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-08.title: Denest the radical
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-08.body:
$15\sqrt8=30\sqrt2$. Look for $(m-n\sqrt2)^2=m^2+2n^2-2mn\sqrt2=43-30\sqrt2$: $mn=15$ and $m^2+2n^2=43$ give $m=5$, $n=3$. Since $5-3\sqrt2>0$, $\sqrt{43-30\sqrt2}=5-3\sqrt2$, so $(a,b,c)=(5,-3,2)$, and indeed $a>c$.

**Answer: $(5,-3,2)$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-09.title: Difference of squares
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-09.body:
Each pair $(2j)^2-(2j-1)^2=4j-1=(2j)+(2j-1)$. So the bracket is $1+2+\dots+2000=\frac{2000\cdot2001}{2}$, and the left side is $2000\cdot2001$.

$k^2+k=k(k+1)=2000\cdot2001$ gives $k=2000$, or $k=-2001$ (since $(-2001)(-2000)$ is the same product).

**Answer: $k=2000$ or $k=-2001$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-10.title: Build from the roots
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-10.body:
From the graph, the polynomial touches the $x$-axis at $-2$ (a double root), crosses it at $2$ and $3$, and passes through $(-1,3)$. So $P(x)=a(x+2)^2(x-2)(x-3)$. At $x=-1$: $a\cdot1\cdot(-3)(-4)=12a=3$, so $a=\frac14$.

The sum of the coefficients is $P(1)=\frac14\cdot9\cdot(-1)(-2)=\frac92$.

**Answer: $\frac92$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-11.title: Complementary angles
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-11.body:
For acute angles, $\sin A=\cos B$ means $A+B=90^\circ$: $x^2+3x+80=90$, so $x^2+3x-10=0$, $(x+5)(x-2)=0$.

Both work: $x=-5$ gives $A=25^\circ$, $B=65^\circ$; $x=2$ gives $A=4^\circ$, $B=86^\circ$.

**Answer: $x=-5$ or $x=2$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-12.title: Common intersection point
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-12.body:
Triangles $GAE$, $EAS$, $ASM$ are equilateral with side $d=GA$. As the figure shows, circles $G$, $A$ and $E$ pass through one common point, which must be equidistant ($r$) from $G$, $A$, $E$: the center of equilateral triangle $GAE$. So the circumradius of the triangle is $r$, and $d=r\sqrt3$.

Along segment $GA$ the two radii overlap by $k=2r-d=(2-\sqrt3)r$, so $\frac kr=2-\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $2-\sqrt3$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-13.title: Sum of cubes identity
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-13.body:
With $b=1000$, $c=999$ and $b+c=1999$: $(b+c)^3-b^3-c^3=3bc(b+c)$. So the fraction is $\frac{3\cdot1000\cdot999\cdot1999}{1999\cdot1000\cdot999}=3$.

**Answer: $3$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-15.title: Four quarter circles
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-15.body:
Inside the square each unit circle covers a quarter disk of area $\frac\pi4$; they touch only at the midpoints of the sides. The remaining area is $4-4\cdot\frac\pi4=4-\pi$.

**Answer: $(4,-1)$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-16.title: Compare the options
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-16.body:
Her $10$ sure answers give $50$ points. If she guesses on $g$ of the other $20$ and omits $20-g$, with $c$ lucky guesses she scores $50+2(20-g)+5c=90-2g+5c$. She needs $5c\ge10+2g$.

Each guess is right with probability $\frac15$. For small $g$:
- $g\le3$: need $c>g$, impossible.
- $g=4$: need $c\ge4$: $\left(\frac15\right)^4=0.0016$.
- $g=5$: need $c\ge4$: $5\left(\frac15\right)^4\frac45+\left(\frac15\right)^5=\frac{21}{3125}\approx0.0067$.
- $g=6$: need $c\ge5$: $\approx0.0016$; $g=7$: need $c\ge5$: $\approx0.0047$.

Larger $g$ require more correct guesses; computing the binomial probabilities for $g=8,\dots,20$ gives at most about $0.0064$ (at $g=10$, needing $c\ge6$). The best choice is $g=5$.

**Answer: $5$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-17.title: Remove the even factors
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-17.body:
$1999!$ is the product of the odd numbers up to $1999$ times the even numbers $2,4,\dots,1998$. The even part is $2\cdot4\cdots1998=2^{999}(1\cdot2\cdots999)=2^{999}\cdot999!$. Hence $1999!!!=\frac{1999!}{2^{999}\cdot999!}$, so $a=999$.

**Answer: $999$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-18.title: Area as a quadratic
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-18.body:
With radius $r$ and arc length $s$: $f=2r+s$ and the area is $\frac12rs=\frac12r(f-2r)=-r^2+\frac f2r$. This quadratic in $r$ is maximized at $r=\frac{f}{4}$.

**Answer: $r=\frac f4$ feet**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-18.title: AM–GM
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-18.body:
Area $=\frac12rs=\frac14(2r)(s)\le\frac14\left(\frac{2r+s}{2}\right)^2=\frac{f^2}{16}$, with equality when $2r=s=\frac f2$, i.e. $r=\frac f4$.

**Answer: $r=\frac f4$ feet**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-20.title: Geometric series
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-20.body:
If the first rectangle has area $S$, the second has area $S\left(1+\frac12+\frac14+\dots\right)=2S$. For similar figures the area ratio is the square of the length ratio, so $k^2=2$ and $k=\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $\sqrt2$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-21.title: Count lines
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-21.body:
There are $3+3+2=8$ winning lines, out of $\binom93=84$ equally likely sets of three boxes. Probability $\frac{8}{84}=\frac{2}{21}$.

**Answer: $\frac2{21}$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-22.title: Find the three points
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-22.body:
The fourth vertex is $P+Q-R$ for each choice of $R$: $(1,5)$, $(-3,1)$, $(5,-1)$. Shoelace:
$$\tfrac12\left|1(1+1)+(-3)(-1-5)+5(5-1)\right|=\tfrac12|2+18+20|=20.$$

**Answer: $20$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-22.title: Medial triangle
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-22.body:
The given triangle is the medial triangle of the triangle formed by the three possible $D$'s, so that triangle has $4$ times the area. The given triangle has area $\frac12|(-1)(2-0)+3(0-3)+1(3-2)|=5$, so the answer is $20$.

**Answer: $20$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-23.title: Eight octants
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-23.body:
Inside the cube each sphere contributes one eighth of a unit ball, and the pieces do not overlap (adjacent centers are $2$ apart). Together they make one unit ball, volume $\frac43\pi$. Remaining volume: $8-\frac43\pi$.

**Answer: $\left(8,-\frac43\right)$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-24.title: One round at a time
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-24.body:
In a round, Tommy wins if Liz fails ($\frac12$), Ralph fails ($\frac23$) and Tommy succeeds ($\frac16$): probability $\frac1{18}$. Nobody wins in a round with probability $\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac56=\frac5{18}$. So
$$P=\frac1{18}\left(1+\frac5{18}+\left(\frac5{18}\right)^2+\dots\right)=\frac{1/18}{13/18}=\frac1{13}.$$

**Answer: $\frac1{13}$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-24.title: Relative weights
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-24.body:
Within a round the first winner is Liz, Ralph or Tommy with weights $\frac12$, $\frac12\cdot\frac13=\frac16$, $\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac16=\frac1{18}$, i.e. $9:3:1$. Rounds repeat identically, so Tommy wins with probability $\frac1{13}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{13}$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-25.title: Subtract termwise
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-25.body:
$\log_2 2k-\log_2 k=\log_2 2=1$ for each $k$, so the difference is $1000\cdot1=1000$.

**Answer: $1000$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-26.title: Shift and subtract
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-26.body:
Let $S$ be the sum. Then $S-\frac S3=\frac13+\frac19+\frac1{27}+\dots=\frac{1/3}{1-1/3}=\frac12$, so $\frac23S=\frac12$ and $S=\frac34$.

**Answer: $\frac34$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-27.title: Factor a difference of squares
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-27.body:
With radii $R>r>0$: $\pi(R^2-r^2)=2000\pi$, so $(R-r)(R+r)=2000$. The factors $R-r$ and $R+r$ have the same parity, and their product is even, so both are even: $R-r=2u$, $R+r=2v$ with $uv=500$ and $u<v$ (then $r=v-u>0$).

$500=2^2\cdot5^3$ has $12$ divisors, giving $6$ pairs with $u<v$: $u=1,2,4,5,10,20$. The distances $R-r=2u$ are $2,4,8,10,20,40$: six possibilities.

**Answer: $6$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-28.title: Determinant, then check consistency
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-28.body:
The coefficient matrix has $k$ on the diagonal and $3$ elsewhere; its determinant is $(k-3)^2(k+6)$. For other $k$ there is a unique solution, so only $k=3$ and $k=-6$ can fail.
- $k=3$: the equations say $3X+3Y+3Z$ equals $1000$, $900$ and $100$ at once: no solution.
- $k=-6$: adding the three equations gives $0=2000$: no solution.

**Answer: $k=3$ or $k=-6$**

nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-29.title: Angle sum
nyciml-1999-00-spring-seniora-29.body:
The angles are $100,110,\dots,100+10(n-1)$, with sum $100n+5n(n-1)$. Setting this equal to $180(n-2)$: $5n^2-85n+360=0$, i.e. $n^2-17n+72=0$, so $n=8$ or $n=9$. For $n=9$ the largest angle would be $180^\circ$, impossible. So $n=8$ (angles $100^\circ$ to $170^\circ$, sum $1080^\circ$).

**Answer: $8$**
